 France Raises Minimum Wage by 1.6 Per Cent amid Cost-of-Living Protests
 CURRENT 
 France Raises Minimum Wage by 1.6 Per Cent amid Cost-of-Living Protests
 Protesters in Paris on 7 November 2026
 Firas Abdullah/MTI/EPA
 France will raise its minimum wage by 1.6 per cent from 1 December, bringing monthly net pay to €1,502, in a move aimed at easing tensions after weeks of cost-of-living protests. 
 Ádám Bráder 
 — 
 10.11.2026 
 The French government announced on Monday that it would raise the minimum wage by 1.6 per cent from 1 December, bringing forward the increase in an effort to ease tensions after weeks of protests over the rising cost of living.
 Reassessing the minimum wage has been one of the demands made by trade unions, which have pointed out that governments have not introduced an increase above the rate of inflation since 2012. The current monthly minimum wage stands at €1,867.02 gross and €1,477.93 net. Under the new measure, net monthly pay will rise by €23.65 to €1,502.
 Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu described the increase as the second-largest in the past 20 years. He made the announcement after meeting with trade union and employer representatives at his office.
 Labour Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou said the government was contributing an additional 0.6 per cent to the increase by bringing it forward by one month. The minimum wage is otherwise adjusted automatically in January in line with inflation.
 ‘Our best estimate of inflation as of 15 December 2026 is currently 1 per cent. Of the announced 1.6 per cent increase, 1 percentage point therefore corresponds to the automatic adjustment. The actual increase is 0.6 per cent,’ Farandou said, describing the government’s contribution as far from negligible.
 Sophie Binet, head of France’s largest trade union, the CGT, dismissed the announcement as inadequate. She said the government had offered workers only ‘crumbs’, adding that €18 of the announced €23 increase corresponded to the automatic adjustment scheduled for 1 January.
 ‘We did not come here to beg for charity, but to demand respect and recognition for our work, and an answer to the enormous social anger being expressed across the country,’ Binet said.
 She called on workers, pensioners and young people to take to the streets again on 17 November, warning that protests would continue until wages increased and unions’ demands were addressed.
 ‘While wages do not rise and our demands remain unanswered, mobilization will continue. Negotiations must now begin everywhere, and they must lead to pay increases,’ she said.
 Marylise Léon, head of the CFDT trade union, also described the 1.6 per cent increase as insufficient following the government’s announcement and a social conference.
